brief.summary: A proposal workspace for small government contracting firms that hands an AI model a public-sector request for proposals and the firm's draft response, and has it build and check the compliance matrix with a page citation for every requirement.
brief.user: Leah Ostrowski, the proposal manager and one of 11 employees at a small engineering and IT services firm that bids on city and county contracts. She has written around 60 public bids and knows that a single missed mandatory form can get a proposal thrown out unread.
brief.moment: The firm is bidding on a city's 84-page RFP for a 311 service request system replacement, due Friday at 2 p.m. Two addenda came out this week. She asked the AI to pull every 'shall' and 'must' requirement from the RFP and both addenda, map each to the section of their 41-page draft that answers it, and flag gaps. It has finished a first pass and found 137 requirements, marking 118 as addressed, 12 as partial and 7 as missing. She needs to check its work before she trusts it: confirm it caught that Addendum 2 changed the insurance minimum, spot any requirements it invented or misread, reject weak mappings, and decide which gaps to send to which colleague.
brief.data: Source documents: RFP No. 2026-114 (84 pages, 9 sections), Addendum 1 (3 pages, Nov 9), Addendum 2 (5 pages, Nov 13, raises general liability minimum from $1M to $2M and adds a local-business participation form), the firm's draft response v6 (41 pages), and 4 required city forms. The AI run: task instructions Leah gave, start time, documents read, 137 extracted requirements each with ID, quoted text, source page and paragraph, mandatory or desirable, mapped draft section and page, status, the model's confidence, and its short reasoning. Leah has already reviewed 22 (accepted 19, corrected 3). Team: 4 colleagues who own sections (technical approach, staffing, pricing, forms). Evaluation weights from the RFP: technical 40, experience 25, price 25, local participation 10.

prompt:
I need the front end for Bidwright. A proposal workspace for small government contracting firms that hands an AI model a public-sector request for proposals and the firm's draft response, and has it build and check the compliance matrix with a page citation for every requirement.

Who's using it: Leah Ostrowski, the proposal manager and one of 11 employees at a small engineering and IT services firm that bids on city and county contracts. She has written around 60 public bids and knows that a single missed mandatory form can get a proposal thrown out unread.

What they're doing right now: The firm is bidding on a city's 84-page RFP for a 311 service request system replacement, due Friday at 2 p.m. Two addenda came out this week. She asked the AI to pull every 'shall' and 'must' requirement from the RFP and both addenda, map each to the section of their 41-page draft that answers it, and flag gaps. It has finished a first pass and found 137 requirements, marking 118 as addressed, 12 as partial and 7 as missing. She needs to check its work before she trusts it: confirm it caught that Addendum 2 changed the insurance minimum, spot any requirements it invented or misread, reject weak mappings, and decide which gaps to send to which colleague.

What's in the system at this point: Source documents: RFP No. 2026-114 (84 pages, 9 sections), Addendum 1 (3 pages, Nov 9), Addendum 2 (5 pages, Nov 13, raises general liability minimum from $1M to $2M and adds a local-business participation form), the firm's draft response v6 (41 pages), and 4 required city forms. The AI run: task instructions Leah gave, start time, documents read, 137 extracted requirements each with ID, quoted text, source page and paragraph, mandatory or desirable, mapped draft section and page, status, the model's confidence, and its short reasoning. Leah has already reviewed 22 (accepted 19, corrected 3). Team: 4 colleagues who own sections (technical approach, staffing, pricing, forms). Evaluation weights from the RFP: technical 40, experience 25, price 25, local participation 10.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
